title: A Voice Note After Finally Fixing My Sleep Schedule
script: Narrator: [tired but proud] Recording this at ten thirty at night, which might sound normal to you, but for me, this is genuinely an achievement.
Narrator: For almost a year, I went to bed around two in the morning, scrolling my phone long after I should have been asleep.
Narrator: [reflective] I always blamed work stress, although honestly, the habit continued even during weeks when work was fairly calm.
Narrator: [embarrassed] The turning point came when I fell asleep during an important meeting, briefly, but long enough for my manager to notice and comment.
Narrator: That was humiliating, and it forced me to admit my sleep schedule wasn't just inconvenient, it was actually affecting my work seriously.
Narrator: [determined] So I made small changes, starting with charging my phone in the kitchen instead of beside my bed every night.
Narrator: [restless] The first few nights were strange. I kept reaching for a phone that simply wasn't there anymore, out of pure habit.
Narrator: [calmly] I also started making a caffeine-free warm drink around nine, a quiet signal to my brain that the day was slowly winding down.
Narrator: [surprised] Within two weeks, I was falling asleep before midnight, which felt almost impossible when I first started this whole experiment.
Narrator: Now, most nights, I'm actually asleep by eleven, and waking up no longer feels like fighting against my own body.
Narrator: [reflective] My mornings changed the most, surprisingly. I used to wake up already exhausted, dragging myself through the first few hours of every day.
Narrator: Now I actually have quiet time before work, enough to eat breakfast slowly instead of rushing out the door.
Narrator: [honestly] I still slip sometimes, especially on weekends, when I convince myself just one more episode won't matter that much.
Narrator: But overall, this small change reshaped my entire day, not only my nights, which I genuinely didn't expect when I started.
Narrator: [carefully] Moving a phone may be one useful experiment. If serious sleepiness or sleep problems continue, seek appropriate health advice instead of relying on one habit.

quiz.question: What was the narrator's old bedtime habit?
options: Never using her phone at night
Going to bed around two in the morning, scrolling her phone
quiz.explanation: She used to go to bed around two in the morning while scrolling her phone.

quiz.question: What was the turning point that made her change her habits?
options: Falling asleep briefly during an important meeting
quiz.explanation: She fell asleep during an important meeting and her manager noticed, which embarrassed her.

quiz.question: What was the first change she made?
options: Charging her phone in the kitchen instead of beside her bed
quiz.explanation: She started charging her phone in the kitchen instead of next to her bed.

quiz.question: What does she do around nine to signal her day is winding down?
quiz.explanation: She started making tea around nine as a quiet signal to wind down.

quiz.question: How have her mornings changed the most?
options: She now has quiet time to eat breakfast slowly instead of rushing
She wakes up later than before
quiz.explanation: She says mornings changed the most, now having quiet time to eat breakfast slowly instead of rushing.

quiz.question: What evidence weakened the work-stress explanation?
options: The phone was used only at work
The late habit continued during calm work weeks
quiz.explanation: The pattern remained when the claimed cause was absent.

quiz.question: Why was falling asleep in the meeting significant?
options: The schedule was affecting daytime function and work
The narrator had finished every task
quiz.explanation: The consequence showed the issue was more than inconvenience.

quiz.question: What role does the warm drink play?
options: It medically treats every sleep problem
It replaces the need for a bedtime
It is a repeated signal that the day is ending
quiz.explanation: A caffeine-free routine supports transition rather than acting as a cure.

quiz.question: How does the narrator respond to occasional slips?
options: She stays awake the next night
She returns to the routine instead of treating one night as failure
quiz.explanation: The story presents improvement as imperfect but continuing.

quiz.question: When is professional advice appropriate?
options: When serious sleepiness or sleep difficulty continues
Only if moving the phone works
Never, because the habit solved it
quiz.explanation: Persistent symptoms may need assessment beyond self-help.
